description: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is the queen of all moles, a complex and deeply flavorful sauce with a rich history. This traditional dish from Oaxaca boasts a symphony of flavors from an array of chiles, nuts, seeds, spices, and a touch of Mexican chocolate. It's truly a labor of love that rewards with an unforgettable culinary experience.

instructions.title: Prepare and Toast Chiles
instructions.text: Carefully wipe the dried chiles clean. Heat a dry comal or skillet over medium-low heat. Toast the chiles one by one for 10-15 seconds per side until fragrant but not burnt. Be careful not to burn them, as this will make the mole bitter. Once toasted, immerse the chiles in hot water for 20-30 minutes until softened. Drain and reserve the soaking liquid.

instructions.title: Roast Aromatics, Nuts, and Spices
instructions.text: On the same comal or skillet, roast the tomatillos, onion, and garlic until lightly charred and softened, about 5-7 minutes. In a separate dry pan, toast the almonds, peanuts, sesame seeds, and pumpkin seeds separately until golden and fragrant. Then, briefly toast the peppercorns, anise seeds, cinnamon, cloves, cumin, thyme, and marjoram until aromatic, about 1-2 minutes. Be mindful not to burn them.

instructions.title: Sauté Remaining Ingredients
instructions.text: Heat 1 tablespoon of oil or lard in a skillet. Fry the raisins until plump, about 1 minute. Add the stale tortilla or bread and fry until golden brown. Drain any excess oil and set aside with the other toasted ingredients.

instructions.title: Blend the Mole Paste
instructions.text: Combine the softened chiles, roasted tomatillos, onion, garlic, toasted nuts, seeds, spices, fried raisins, and fried tortilla/bread in a blender. Add about 2 cups of the reserved chile soaking liquid and chicken broth. Blend until incredibly smooth. This may require working in batches and blending for several minutes, pushing down solids as needed. Strain the paste through a fine-mesh sieve into a large bowl, pressing down on the solids to extract all liquid. Discard any remaining solids.

instructions.title: Cook the Mole Sauce
instructions.text: In a large heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, heat the remaining oil or lard over medium heat. Carefully pour in the strained mole paste. It will splatter, so be cautious. Cook the mole, stirring constantly, for at least 30-45 minutes. This step is crucial for developing the deep flavors. The mole will darken and thicken significantly. Continue stirring to prevent sticking.

instructions.title: Season and Finish the Mole
instructions.text: Gradually stir in the remaining hot chicken broth, about 1 cup at a time, until the mole reaches your desired consistency. It should be thick enough to coat the back of a spoon. Add the chopped Mexican chocolate and stir until it completely melts into the sauce. Season with salt to taste, and if needed, a pinch of sugar to balance the bitterness of the chiles and chocolate. Simmer for another 20-30 minutes, allowing the flavors to meld beautifully.

instructions.title: Combine with Chicken and Serve
instructions.text: Add the pre-cooked chicken pieces to the simmering mole sauce. Gently stir to ensure the chicken is fully coated. Continue to simmer for 10-15 minutes, allowing the chicken to absorb the rich flavors and heat through. Serve hot with warm corn tortillas, white rice, and a sprinkle of sesame seeds for garnish. Enjoy this masterpiece!

tips: Toasting the chiles properly is key: do it quickly on a dry comal until fragrant, but never burnt, or your mole will be bitter.
For an even richer flavor, use chicken fat (rendered lard) instead of vegetable oil when cooking the mole paste.
Mole freezes beautifully. Make a large batch and freeze portions for a quick and authentic Mexican meal anytime.
article:
Discover the Soul of Oaxaca: Mastering Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole

Embark on a culinary journey to the heart of Oaxaca, Mexico, where food is not just sustenance but a vibrant expression of culture, history, and community. Among its many gastronomic treasures, one dish stands supreme: Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole. This isn't just a sauce; it's a symphony of flavors, a labor of love, and a testament to centuries of culinary tradition. Often reserved for the most special occasions, from weddings to patron saint festivals, making Mole Negro at home is an act of devotion, rewarding the patient cook with an unparalleled depth of taste that transforms any meal into an unforgettable feast. If you're looking for an authentic Mexican dinner recipe that truly impresses, look no further.

## What is Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole?

Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is arguably the most complex and revered of Oaxaca's famed "seven moles." Its distinctive dark, almost black color, comes from a meticulous process of charring chiles, spices, and seeds, creating an unparalleled depth of flavor that is smoky, sweet, spicy, and earthy all at once. This isn't a quick sauce; it's a slow-cooked masterpiece, often taking days to prepare in traditional Oaxacan kitchens. At its core, Mole Negro is a rich, thick sauce made from a bewildering array of ingredients, typically including several types of dried chiles (such as chilhuacle negro, mulato, pasilla, and ancho), nuts, seeds, spices, fruits, aromatics, and a crucial touch of Mexican chocolate.

The history of mole dates back to pre-Hispanic times, with indigenous communities grinding various ingredients to create complex sauces. With the arrival of the Spanish, new ingredients like nuts, seeds, and spices were introduced, evolving mole into the sophisticated dish we know today. In Oaxaca, each family often has its own guarded recipe, passed down through generations, making every Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole a unique culinary signature. It represents celebration, community, and the profound culinary heritage of Mexico.

## Ingredients You Need

Preparing an authentic Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole requires a commitment to sourcing a diverse range of ingredients. While the list might seem long, each component plays a vital role in building the sauce's legendary complexity.

*   **The Chiles (the heart of the mole):** At least six varieties are ideal, with chilhuacle negro being the most traditional and coveted for its smoky, raisin-like notes. Other essential chiles include mulato, pasilla Oaxaca (or pasilla mexicano), ancho, chilcostle, and even a few arbol chiles for a subtle kick. Ensure they are dried and pliable.
*   **Aromatics:** White onion, garlic cloves, ripe tomatoes (or tomatillos), and plantains (or ripe bananas) contribute sweetness and body.
*   **Nuts and Seeds:** Almonds, peanuts, pecans, sesame seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and sometimes even walnuts or cashews, provide richness, texture, and help thicken the sauce.
*   **Spices:** Aromatic spices like cinnamon stick, cloves, black peppercorns, cumin seeds, coriander seeds, oregano (Mexican oregano preferred), and thyme are crucial for depth.
*   **Thickeners/Fruits:** Raisins, prunes, or other dried fruits add sweetness and body. A slice of bread or a tortilla can also be toasted and added for thickening.
*   **Chocolate:** Authentic Mexican chocolate, typically unsweetened or very dark, is essential. It adds richness and a subtle bitterness, balancing the other flavors, not making the mole taste overtly sweet like a dessert.
*   **Broth:** Chicken or turkey broth is traditionally used, providing a savory liquid base for the sauce. Vegetable broth can be used for a vegetarian version.
*   **Fat:** Lard or a neutral oil (like canola or vegetable oil) for toasting and frying.
*   **Seasoning:** Salt and piloncillo (Mexican brown sugar) or regular brown sugar to balance flavors.

## Step-by-Step Instructions

Making Mole Negro is a journey, not a sprint. Break it down into these manageable steps:

1.  **Prepare the Chiles:** Destem and deseed all the dried chiles. Gently toast them in a dry pan over medium heat for 30-60 seconds per side until fragrant but not burnt (burnt chiles will make the mole bitter). Submerge the toasted chiles in hot water for about 20-30 minutes until softened. Drain, reserving the soaking liquid.
2.  **Toast Nuts, Seeds, and Spices:** In a dry pan, toast the sesame seeds until lightly golden. Remove and set aside. Then, toast the almonds, peanuts, and other nuts/seeds separately until lightly browned. In the same pan, toast the whole spices (cinnamon, cloves, peppercorns, cumin, coriander) until fragrant.
3.  **Sauté Aromatics and Fruits:** Heat lard or oil in a large pot or skillet. Sauté the chopped onion and garlic until softened. Add the tomatoes (or tomatillos) and cook until they soften and release their juices. Add the plantain slices and any dried fruits, cooking until slightly caramelized.
4.  **Assemble and Blend the Paste:** Combine the rehydrated chiles, toasted nuts, seeds, spices, sautéed aromatics, and a small amount of the reserved chile soaking liquid (or broth) in a blender. Blend in batches until a very smooth, thick paste forms. This may take several minutes per batch, and you might need to add more liquid gradually to aid blending, but avoid making it too watery.
5.  **Fry the Paste (The Crucial Step):** In a very large, heavy-bottomed pot or Dutch oven, heat a generous amount of lard or oil over medium-high heat. Carefully add the mole paste (it will splatter, so be cautious). Fry the paste, stirring constantly with a sturdy spoon, for at least 20-30 minutes. This step is critical; it deepens the flavor and darkens the color of the Mole Negro, transforming raw flavors into a harmonious blend. The paste will thicken and darken considerably.
6.  **Simmer with Broth and Chocolate:** Gradually add the chicken or turkey broth to the fried paste, stirring continuously to prevent lumps. Bring the mixture to a gentle simmer. Add the Mexican chocolate, breaking it into pieces, and stir until it fully melts and incorporates.
7.  **Season and Finish:** Continue to simmer the mole over low heat for at least 1 to 2 hours, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking. The sauce should thicken to a rich, velvety consistency, coating the back of a spoon. Taste and adjust seasoning with salt and piloncillo (or brown sugar) until the flavors are perfectly balanced – a complex interplay of smoky, sweet, spicy, and earthy notes. If the mole is too thick, add a little more broth. If it's too thin, simmer longer.
8.  **Serve:** Add your cooked protein (chicken, turkey, pork) directly into the simmering mole during the last 30 minutes of cooking, allowing it to absorb the incredible flavors.

## Pro Tips for the Best Results

*   **Source Authentic Chiles:** The chilhuacle negro is key to the unique flavor of Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole. If unavailable, use a combination of mulato, ancho, and pasilla Oaxaca, but be aware the flavor profile will differ slightly.
*   **Don't Rush the Toasting:** Each ingredient needs careful attention during toasting. Burnt chiles or nuts will impart a bitter taste to the entire mole. Toast until fragrant, not charred.
*   **Blend Thoroughly:** A truly smooth mole requires patience with your blender. Blend in small batches if necessary, and consider straining the finished mole through a fine-mesh sieve for an ultra-smooth consistency, though many traditional cooks skip this for a more rustic texture.
*   **The "Frying" Step is Non-Negotiable:** This prolonged cooking of the paste in fat is what develops the deep, complex flavors and characteristic dark color. Do not skip or shorten this step.
*   **Patience is a Virtue:** Mole is a slow food. The long simmering time allows the myriad flavors to meld and deepen. Plan to dedicate a significant amount of time to its preparation.
*   **Taste and Adjust:** Mole is about balance. Constantly taste and adjust salt, sweetness, and even a touch of acidity (like a splash of vinegar or a squeeze of lime) if needed, to bring out the best in the sauce.
*   **Make Ahead:** Mole tastes even better the next day! Its flavors deepen and meld overnight. It can be made days in advance or frozen for future use.

## Serving Suggestions

Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole is most traditionally served with poultry. Chicken and turkey are classic choices, their mild flavors providing the perfect canvas for the mole's richness. Simply braise or roast your poultry and then simmer it in the mole sauce until heated through and coated.

Accompanying sides are usually simple to let the mole shine:
*   **White Rice:** A staple, perfectly soaking up the rich sauce.
*   **Warm Corn Tortillas:** Essential for scooping up every last drop of mole.
*   **Mexican Red Rice:** Another popular choice, offering a slightly different flavor profile.
*   **Garnishes:** A sprinkle of toasted sesame seeds, fresh cilantro, or thinly sliced red onion can add texture and a pop of color.

For a more elaborate meal, serve with a side of refried beans or a simple salad to cut through the richness.

## Variations and Substitutions

While the traditional Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole recipe is sacred, there are some practical adjustments you can make:

*   **Chile Substitutions:** If chilhuacle negro is impossible to find, increase the quantities of mulato and ancho chiles, as they offer similar dark, fruity notes. A smoked pasilla (pasilla Oaxaca) can also contribute a smoky depth.
*   **Nut/Seed Variations:** Feel free to experiment with different nuts and seeds based on availability and preference. Pecans or walnuts can add a different layer of richness.
*   **Vegetarian/Vegan Mole:** Omit the chicken broth and use vegetable broth instead. Ensure no lard is used in the frying process (use oil). Serve over roasted vegetables (like sweet potatoes, cauliflower, or mushrooms), plantains, or even hearty beans and rice.
*   **Sweetness/Spice Level:** Adjust the amount of piloncillo or sugar to your taste. For more heat, include a few extra arbol chiles or a pinch of chipotle powder. For less heat, carefully remove all seeds from the chiles.
*   **Shortcuts (with caution):** Some pre-made mole pastes are available in specialty Mexican markets. While they can save time, they rarely achieve the depth and complexity of a homemade Mole Negro Oaxacan Black Mole. If using a paste, you'll still need to fry it and add broth and chocolate.

Making Mole Negro is an unforgettable culinary adventure. It’s a dish that teaches patience, rewards effort, and connects you to a rich cultural heritage. Enjoy the process, savor the aromas, and relish the incredible flavors of this iconic Mexican dinner recipe.
